paragraphs: I want to inquire whether, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule of administration, taking men as they are and laws as they might be. In this inquiry I shall always try to unite what right permits with what interest requires, so that justice and utility are never divided.

I begin my task without arguing that the subject is important. I shall be asked whether I am a prince or a legislator, that I write about politics. I answer that I am neither, and that is why I write. If I were a prince or a legislator, I would not waste my time saying what needs doing; I would do it, or keep quiet.

Because I was born a citizen of a free State and a member of the Sovereign, I feel that, however weak the influence of my voice on public affairs may be, the right to vote on them makes it my duty to study them. And I am happy, whenever I reflect on governments, to find that my inquiries always give me new reasons to love the government of my own country.

Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. One man thinks himself the master of others, yet remains a greater slave than they are. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? That question I think I can answer.

If I considered only force and the effects that flow from it, I would say: “As long as a people is compelled to obey, and obeys, it does well; as soon as it can shake off the yoke, and does so, it does better still. For in regaining its liberty by the same right that took it away, either it is justified in taking it back, or there was no justification for those who took it away.” But the social order is a sacred right that is the basis of all other rights. Yet this right does not come from nature, and so it must be founded on conventions. Before turning to that, I must prove what I have just asserted.
